name: VTE risk pregnancy
seoTitle: VTE risk pregnancy — Free Online Calculator
seoDesc: VTE risk pregnancy: work out weight from the height and the BMI. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The VTE risk pregnancy calculator turns the height and the BMI into weight. That makes it useful for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the VTE risk pregnancy calculator work?
sections.html:
The VTE risk pregnancy calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports weight in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the patient's current situation); then you type in the height, the BMI, the result pregnant and the result born.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as patient is pregnant and patient has given birth. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in kg/m^2.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient is over 35 years old”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Previously had venous thromboembolism (VTE)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Previously had VTE provoked by a major surgery”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Has known high-risk thrombophilia due to antithrombin or protein C or S deficiency, compound or homozygous for low-risk thrombophilia”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Has other medical comorbidities (e.g., cancer, heart failure, active systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Has a family history of unprovoked or estrogen-related VTE in a first-degree relative”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Has known low-risk thrombophilia - no VTE: heterozygous for factor V Leiden or prothrombin G20210A mutations”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient has already given birth three times or more”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient is a smoker”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient has gross varicose veins”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient has pre-eclampsia in the current pregnancy”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Assisted reproductive technology (ART) or in vitro fertilization (IVF) was used to achieve pregnancy”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient has multiple pregnancies or twins, triplets, etc”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient had a cesarean section in labor”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Cesarean section was elective or known to the patient before labor”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Has undergone mid-cavity or rotational operative delivery”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Experienced prolonged labor of more than 24 hours”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient had postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) of more than 1 liter and required a transfusion”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.

  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Stillbirth occurred in the current pregnancy”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Patient has undergone any surgical procedure in pregnancy or puerperium”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.

The form has 28 fields in total. The ones not listed here work the same way: a label, a unit chip where the quantity has units, and a box that updates the results as soon as it holds a valid number.

26 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the VTE risk pregnancy calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Weight=BMI × (height ^ 2)
Ohss=-please tick all that apply... − art − comorbidity − emesis − family history − high thrombophilia − immobility − infection − low thrombophilia − multiple − parity − preeclampsia − previous − previous major + result pregnant − smoker − surgery − veins − (BMI)
Immobility=-please tick all that apply... − cesarean section − comorbidity − elective cc − family history − high thrombophilia − infection − low thrombophilia − multiple − operative − parity − pph − preeclampsia − preterm − previous − previous major − prolonged + result born − smoker − stillbirth − surgery − veins − (BMI)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Patient's current situation set to Patient is pregnant, Height = 30 m and BMI = 10. The calculator returns Weight = 0.9 kg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Weight = 0.9 kg should be roughly the size you expected from Patient's current situation set to Patient is pregnant and Height = 30 m.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The VTE risk pregnancy calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the height and the BMI — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the VTE risk pregnancy calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns weight, derived from the height and the BMI. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the VTE risk pregnancy calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the height and the BMI, which is 28 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (26 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Weight = 0.9 kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the VTE risk pregnancy calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
